event: VXE 829 (LRR) pitched up and spun right during VTOL descent at about 100 ft AGL and hit the ground, damaging the aircraft.
failure_mode: ESC microcontroller code corruption locked up the ESC so the motor stopped during landing with throttle still commanded; reflashing the ESC cleared the fault
contributing: Suspected high current, voltage transients and shared microcontroller and power return paths on the heritage ESC
High throttle (about 95 percent for 45 s) on takeoff
Motor 3 did not home its prop after shutdown
Out of tolerance VTOL prop balance (MAG 0.10 vs 0.05)

evidence.quote: Removed right aft lift motor and ESC from boom, no obvious problems found.
I managed to replicate the fault. I found that during the landing phase even with the throttle active, motor stops running. I flashed the ESC again and fault went away.
9/22 After several runs of AAR flight profiles, we were able to replicate the fault mode observed during the flight incident.
@Drew Hildreth @Pat Wells Eric looked at the log and the GPS fault was a side effect o the failure, vehicle tilt caused satellite loss, which triggered the message (correctly, but uselessly).
I ran the throttle 3 (Right rear motor) profile on dyno using two motors, the 829 motor and a known good motor.

team_root_cause:
- ESC microcontroller code corruption. Suspect caused by high current, voltage transients, and shared return paths of microcontroller and power on the ESC.
- The VTOL ESCs are exposed to intense conditions during launch and landing. A small percentage of ESCs will pass all initial tests and develop latent failures that could not have been caught during initial checkouts. The corrective actions listed below should help with earlier detection and reduce the occurrence of such failures.

would_settle_it.what: Dyno replication data and the analysis of what corrupted the ESC image
A readback of the corrupted ESC flash compared with the golden image would confirm corruption and show which region changed

would_settle_it.file: Laszlo Juhasz analysis recommending not using the processor in ESC applications
would_settle_it.what: Lift ESC design issues that would explain how the ESC processor code was corrupted

attachments_read: 31373_RMA Quote to Repair VXE-829 Warranty Edge Asset 250811-1 August 11, 2025.pdf.md
reasoning: The aircraft spun right during VTOL descent and the right aft (motor 3) motor and ESC were pulled for test. On the dyno, running the incident flight profile reproduced the motor stopping during the landing stage with throttle active, and reflashing the ESC made the fault go away, which points to corrupted ESC microcontroller code rather than the motor windings. The GPS fault was shown to be a side effect of the high attitude. The cause of the corruption (transients, shared returns) remains a suspicion.
notes: Position: ticket uses right aft, right rear and motor 3 (right rear) for the same unit, mapped to motor 3 (rear right). Earlier comments suspected the motor (higher temperature, back EMF waveform, phase current) and one status note says ESC 4 ran hot; the later replication and reflash result supersede these. Motor 2 grinding noise judged not causal. The investigation report and Word summary are on SharePoint and not in the export. Linked ticket VXEP-628 read at review: the systemic ESC tracker lists VXEP-1464 with cause "Processor corruption" and asks for a prior analysis recommending not using the processor in ESC applications, which agrees with this result; no change to the result.

event: VXE 827 (LRR) aborted its first VTOL launch on a laser range finder fault and GPS fault, drifted in manual nudge and landed on its own without damage.
component: GPS position solution (uncertainty above launch threshold)
failure_mode: GPS uncertainty during launch triggered a designed launch abort; LRF return was unstable at the abort altitude, giving a second fault message
contributing: Joystick was unplugged, so the pilot's pause and nudge commands were not taken
Failed calibration and power cycle during preflight

evidence.quote: System operating as expected. Uncertainty in GPS resulted in abort of the launch (this is normal).
Due to the altitude at which the abort occurred, the LRF return was unstable which resulted in the additional error message.
These commands were not taken by the aircraft because the joystick was unplugged.
During the preflight of this aircraft, there was a failed calibration. After this failed calibration, the aircraft was power cycled.

team_root_cause: System operating as expected. Uncertainty in GPS resulted in abort of the launch (this is normal). Due to the altitude at which the abort occurred, the LRF return was unstable which resulted in the additional error message.

would_settle_it.what: Log plot of GPS uncertainty against the abort threshold at the time of the abort
Why GPS uncertainty rose (satellite count, CN0, interference) and the LRF return at abort altitude

reasoning: The engineers state the launch was aborted because GPS uncertainty rose, which is designed behavior, and the LRF fault was a side effect of the abort altitude. Under the designed abort rule this is scored on the degraded input, the GPS solution. Why the GPS uncertainty rose is not explained in the ticket.
notes: Only evidence beyond the Root Cause field is an embedded log image that was not converted. Operator issue (joystick unplugged) contributed to the uncontrolled drift but not to the abort.

event: VXE 732 (TIQUILA) fuel cell was found off after a Land Now descent with about 100 g of propane left; the landing itself was normal.
component: VSM (OGCS) Land Immediately fuel cell shutoff logic
failure_mode: VSM sent a fuel cell shutdown command when Land Immediately was commanded, copying legacy GCS logic that was actually commented out in legacy GCS
contributing: Earlier start failures from a stuck manifold pressure regulator (fixed before flight, not causal)
HLB run below 20 percent during startup

evidence.quote: @Cody Smisek The “Land Immediately” workflow triggers this behavior, just like with Jennings GCS.
@Craig Burton We just tested this on a HIL using legacy GCS (advanced Nav 30 type 115) and did not observe this behavior (no observed commands from GCS to aircraft to shut down fuel cell).
Logs indicate a fuel cell that is operating nominally. Fuel cell shutoff during land immediately as commanded by VSM (unexpected but as designed).
This has been fixed and merged into the VSM’s develop branch that will become a part of OGCS 1.4.
VSM:  Fuel Cell should remain On after Land Immediately is commanded

team_root_cause: During VTOL land immediately, VSM commanded fuel cell shut off (as designed). The intended design was to follow legacy GCS logic, however it was discovered legacy GCS had similar logic commented out.
reasoning: AAR review showed the fuel cell producing power normally with no sign of fuel starvation. The VSM developer confirmed the Land Immediately workflow commands fuel cell shutoff, and a HIL test on legacy GCS showed no such command because those lines were commented out there. The VSM logic was changed (MS-1276) for OGCS 1.4.
notes: VXEP-1476 is a duplicate report of the same event (same text, canceled).

event: Three LRR LEMB chargers (Stalker 28V, S/N 0007, 0013, 0024) smoked when being plugged into their power supplies during training; no fire.
component: Stalker 28V battery charger input DCDC converter
failure_mode: Input DCDC chip failed when the charger input power dropped out below battery voltage while the battery was connected and charging, backfeeding the DCDC
contributing: Charger software had no brownout protection (fixed in V1.2.35, BAT-101)
AC input unplugged and replugged after a FAULT without removing the battery
Power strip breaker tripping earlier that day

evidence.quote: Physical damage on each of the three received chargers matches a condition where the following conditions all existed:
- The input power to the charger experienced a dropout, or loss of voltage below the battery voltage (21-29.4V)
This is an example of improper usage that may result in the observed failures - especially if the charger was attempting to charge the battery when the “FAULT” occurred.
@Addison Osborn , my initial suspicion is that humidity was not a factor here, but I need more information to determine the root cause.
Testing passed on all three chargers with version 1.2.35 of the charger software.  Released to chargers in HSV, and updated on 9/4/25

team_view_in_comments: Physical damage on each of the three received chargers matches a condition where the following conditions all existed:

would_settle_it.what: Failed input DCDC chip on the charger board, confirming the failure location

reasoning: Teardown of all three returned chargers showed damage to the input power DCDC chip matching an input dropout while a battery was connected and charging. An instructor confirmed at least one case where AC input was unplugged and replugged after a FAULT without removing the battery, and the breaker had tripped earlier that day. The charger software was changed to detect brownouts and passed a dropout test on three chargers, which supports the mechanism.
notes: No Root Cause field. The field users' accounts conflict on whether each failure involved a power dropout (one charger smoked while being plugged in with no charging active), so the operator action is confirmed for only one instance. RMA tickets for the three chargers hold no findings. Humidity, the reporter's first guess, was judged not a factor.

failure_mode: OGCS backend server crashed in flight and did not restart, appearing to the crew as lost communications
contributing: Simultaneous comms interruption of at least 4 minutes on both 818 and 828
Docker containers not set to restart after abnormal exit
Docker and NGINX logs not captured in the AAR

evidence.quote: All evidence points to the backend having crashed during flight, though this is not conclusive.
That’s correct, the exact cause of the crash (i.e. offending module or line of code) is still unknown.
- We were missing critical docker and NGINX logs that might've shed more light on the issue.
we cold still see the Silvius webpage, SA camera, and Epsilon so the coms at that point were okay besides the OGCS

team_root_cause: All evidence points to the OGCS backend server having crashed during flight.  This would appear to the user like a lost communications.

would_settle_it.what: OGCS backend exit status and the last log lines before the crash

would_settle_it.file: Photo of error when trying to log in..jpg
would_settle_it.what: The login error shown after the comms loss, which may name the failed backend service

event: TIQUILA testing on GCS 6.5.0 found that the automatic mission simulation run on an RTB command often drew a spiral or braided path that missed IP1, while the aircraft actually flew the expected landing pattern.
failure_mode: RTB-triggered mission simulation displays an erroneous spiral or wide path that does not match the route the aircraft flies
contributing: Possibly introduced with v6.4 and its new compiler toolchain (engineer belief, not confirmed)

evidence.quote: When ever I continued the RTB the AV continued its flight ignoring the spiral and headed to IP1 then 2 and so on.

Aircraft in flight at O3. PLZ is a straight-in approach. PLZ is the active LZ. Aircraft commanded to RTB. Sim is automatically run. Sim generates a bizarre braided orbit which eventually skips IP1 and flies the rest of the pattern.
Aircraft in flight at O3. Both PLZ and ELZ are straight-in approaches. ELZ is the active LZ. A Sim is manually commanded and the results are as expected.
Note: the aircraft will not actually fly the erroneous simulation, it will fly the expected route if allowed to continue.
@Pat Wells I believe it started with v6.4, but I am not positive. It may be related to the new compiler toolchain that was introduced then. Ted is looking into it.

would_settle_it.what: Screen captures of the spiral RTB simulation for comparison with the flown track
LM email text, which did not convert to readable text, may describe further conditions
Why the automatic RTB sim differs from a manually commanded sim from the same aircraft state

reasoning: The regression slides show the automatic RTB simulation drawing braided or very wide paths while a manually commanded sim from the same state is correct, and the customer saw the aircraft fly the proper pattern regardless. VXEP-1477, which an engineer called the same issue, states this is a known GCS simulation component problem the aircraft does not fly. The fault is therefore in the GCS simulation display, but no mechanism was identified.
notes: No comments and no Root Cause field on this ticket; the engineering view is on VXEP-1477 (David Grosher). Five of the six converted PDFs are unreadable glyph codes (font encoding failure); only the pptx text was usable. The related real flight-path issue (missed IP1 on lost link RTB) is VXEP-1479.

event: In TIQUILA HIL simulation (VXE-765 setup) a lost link RTB from about 20 km out made the aircraft skip IP1 and descend toward IP2, reproduced on 6.5.0 and 6.5.1 by Edge on a BLK30 HIL.
failure_mode: Waypoint capture logic falsely captured IP1 when it was about 19.98 km (and multiples) away, so the aircraft moved on to IP2 prematurely
contributing: IP1 placed beyond the aircraft trajectory with PLZ about 20 to 23 km away
Terrain between aircraft and IP2 could cause ground collision with the skipped high IP1 leg

evidence.quote: I reconnected the vehicle to the GCS while flying to track the vehicle path and it still performed as described (missed IP1 waypoint).
We re ran this again with the same results, part way of the journey to IP1 the active landing moved to IP2, We left the AV flying until it landed.
Waypoint capture logic is flawed at 19.98km and factors of 2 distances greater than that resulting in premature capture of waypoints at any point in the mission plan.
@Jackson Riley Curvin This is resolved with v6.6

team_root_cause: Waypoint capture logic is flawed at 19.98km and factors of 2 distances greater than that resulting in premature capture of waypoints at any point in the mission plan.

would_settle_it.file: ENG or FS2 v6.6 FWAP change record
would_settle_it.what: The code change for the waypoint capture fix, which would show the 19.98 km mechanism directly

reasoning: The customer and Edge both reproduced the aircraft skipping IP1 on a lost link RTB with the landing zone about 20 km away, and the VSM log showed landing detected while still flying to IP1. The team named a waypoint capture flaw at 19.98 km and multiples, and the issue was resolved by an FWAP change in v6.6. The mechanism is stated only in the Root Cause field, so confidence is medium.
notes: Tail field is the TIQUILA HIL setup labelled VXE-765 (HIL SIM), not a flying aircraft. Corrective Action field says log bug, likely meaning logic. The two PDFs converted to no text (images only).
